title: Visualising Solid Shapes
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with common 3D shapes — cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere, prism, pyramid.
Idea of 2D shapes (faces) that make up 3D solids.
Comfort with counting and simple arithmetic.

topics.title: Faces, Edges, Vertices & Nets of Solids
topics.quick_summary: Every 3D solid can be described by its number of flat faces, straight edges, and corner vertices, and can be 'unfolded' into a flat 2D net that folds back into the same solid.

detailed.definition: A face is a flat (or curved) surface of a solid; an edge is a line segment where two faces meet; a vertex is a point where edges meet (a corner). A net is a 2D pattern that can be folded to form a 3D solid.
detailed.key_idea: The same solid can often be represented by more than one valid net (different unfolding arrangements), but a net must fold up without gaps or overlaps to correctly form the target solid.
detailed.working_principle: To identify a net correctly, mentally (or physically) fold each flat piece along its shared edges and check whether all faces align correctly to enclose a solid shape with no missing or overlapping surfaces.
applications: Packaging design (boxes, cartons) relies entirely on correct nets for manufacturing folded containers.
Visualizing cross-sections and different views (top, front, side) of solids in engineering and architecture drawings.

topics.real_life: Unfolding a cereal box flat gives its net — a 2D pattern of six rectangles — which can be refolded to reconstruct the original cuboid.
points: A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges, and 8 vertices.
A cuboid also has 6 faces, 12 edges, and 8 vertices (but faces are rectangles, not all squares).
A cylinder has 2 flat circular faces + 1 curved surface, 2 edges, and 0 vertices.
A cone has 1 flat circular face + 1 curved surface, 1 edge, and 1 vertex (the apex).
mistakes: Miscounting curved surfaces as 'no face' — a curved surface still counts as one face for solids like cylinders and cones.
Drawing a net where faces overlap or leave gaps when mentally folded, making it invalid.
Confusing edges (line segments) with vertices (corner points) when describing a solid.
topics.memory_hook: 'Fold it flat, that's the net; count faces, edges, corners for the ID' — every solid has its own fixed count.
topics.advanced: The idea of a 'net' generalises beautifully in higher mathematics to unfolding four-dimensional shapes into three- dimensional nets (a famous example being the 'unfolded tesseract') — the same folding logic used here for cubes and cuboids extends conceptually into shapes we cannot directly visualize.

topics.title: Euler's Formula for Solids
topics.quick_summary: For any convex polyhedron (a solid with flat polygonal faces), the number of faces, vertices, and edges are always related by the simple formula F + V − E = 2.

detailed.definition: A polyhedron is a 3D solid bounded entirely by flat polygonal faces (like a cube, prism, or pyramid); Euler's formula states that for any such convex polyhedron, F + V − E = 2, where F = number of faces, V = number of vertices, and E = number of edges.
detailed.key_idea: Euler's formula acts as a quick consistency check — if a claimed polyhedron's face, vertex, and edge counts don't satisfy F + V − E = 2, either the counts are wrong or the shape isn't a valid simple convex polyhedron.
detailed.working_principle: Count the faces (F), vertices (V), and edges (E) of the solid carefully, then substitute into F + V − E and confirm the result equals 2 for any valid, simple, convex polyhedron.
applications: Verifying structural designs in architecture (domes, trusses) built from polyhedral panels.
Cross-checking answers in geometry problems that describe a solid using only some of F, V, E and ask you to find the missing one.

topics.real_life: Checking a football (soccer ball) pattern of pentagons and hexagons, or verifying a geodesic dome's structural design, both use Euler's formula to confirm the face-edge-vertex count is consistent.
points: Euler's Formula: F + V − E = 2, for any simple convex polyhedron.
Euler's formula does NOT apply to solids with curved surfaces (like cylinders, cones, spheres) since they are not polyhedra.
mistakes: Applying Euler's formula to solids with curved faces (cylinder, cone, sphere) — it is valid only for polyhedra with flat faces.
Miscounting shared edges between faces, leading to an incorrect E value.
Rearranging the formula incorrectly when solving for a missing quantity (e.g., writing E = F + V + 2 instead of E = F + V − 2).
topics.memory_hook: 'Faces plus Vertices, minus Edges, always 2' — a universal fingerprint of any convex polyhedron.
topics.advanced: Euler's formula is one of the earliest results in topology — the branch of mathematics studying properties that don't change under stretching or bending; remarkably, F + V − E = 2 stays true no matter how a polyhedron is distorted (as long as it isn't torn or given a hole), because it reflects a deeper topological property of the sphere- like surface rather than just simple counting.

formulas.name: Euler's Formula
formulas.variables: F = number of faces, V = number of vertices, E = number of edges of a simple convex polyhedron.
formulas.when_to_use: To verify consistency of a polyhedron's face/vertex/edge counts, or to find one missing value given the other two.
formulas.common_mistakes: Applying this to non-polyhedral (curved) solids, or miscounting shared edges/vertices.
formulas.shortcut: Rearrange as needed: E = F + V − 2, or V = 2 − F + E, depending on which quantity is missing.
